**Windows of developmental sensitivity to social media** (URL: [www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-29296-3](http://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-29296-3))  
*(Published Mar 2022\)*

*Summary, Context, & Limitations*

* Analysis suggests that **there are “distinct developmental windows of sensitivity to social media in adolescence**,” when higher estimated social media use predicts a decrease in life satisfaction ratings one year later (and vice-versa: lower estimated social media use predicts an increase in life satisfaction ratings)”  
    * **Differences** were also found between **at which ages** these windows occurred **based on sex**  
* Authors argue that “much needed progress in understanding how social media use affects well-being could be made by” looking at impact of different developmental stages/processes on social media’s effects (especially given mixed results of other social media-well being relationship investigations)  
* Based on **sociocultural changes and life events common in adolescence**, “it is … plausible that \[this **heighten**s\] **adolescents’ sensitivity to the interactive, communicative, and self-portraying nature of social media**”  
    * Especially significant because it is “a technology they use more extensively than other age groups”  
    * Given the “diverse and protracted developmental processes experienced” during adolescence, it makes sense that periods of increased sensitivity to effects of social media would vary throughout different ages within adolescence as well as compared to children/adults  
        * These periods of sensitivity are the windows study examined  
    * Due to variation in some parts of adolescent developmental processes between males and females, sex was also a factor the study examined in social media-well being correlation  
* Limitations of study: wide variety of variables for something as broad as “life satisfaction” (SES/class was factored in as a control but if other major variables exist would confound correlation in windows found by authors), self-report data & ratings which can be biased or differ objectively between individuals


*Research Question/Part 1*

* Study first analyzed relationship between estimated social media use and life satisfaction ratings, grouping results by age.   
    * Used data from the UK Understanding Society household panel survey—”includes 72,287 10-80 year-old participants surveyed up to seven times each between 2011 and 2018”  
        * Found that “**the most substantial negative relations were found in adolescence**,” supporting idea that developmental processes impact social media’s relationship to user well-being  
        * Note that “the relations in the raw data differed when comparing younger (10-15 years) and older adolescents (16-21 years … ),” showing that **the effects (and therefore healthy approaches to) social media differ based on whether adolescent users are younger or older**   
        * Amongst “older” (16-21 y.o.) adolescents, “those who estimated they engaged in very low or very high social media use reported lower life satisfaction ratings than those who estimated that they used between ‘less than an hour’ and ‘1-3 h’ of social media a day”   
            * This relationship has been called “**Goldilocks hypothesis,” claiming individuals with least and most SMS use report lowest well-being ratings**  
        * However, **amongst “younger” adolescents the Goldilocks hypothesis relationship did not occur**, with a linear rather than quadratic relationship between SMS use and life (dis)satisfaction  
            * Also **younger adolescents “showed more prominent differences between males and females” in SMS impact on life satisfaction**  
                * Seems to line up with female developmental processes occurring earlier in adolescence than male ones. Whereas for older adolescents both females and males would have experienced similar developmental processes already, so logically the difference in SMS effect would be less  
                * An Akaike weights procedure performed in the study “showed that **adolescence is unique due to the prominent sex differences on the cross-sectional links between estimated social media use and ratings of life satisfaction that are not evident at most other ages**”   
                    * Further supports idea that developmental processes in adolescence are what drive “sensitivity windows” the authors theorized  
    * Supplemented findings with analysis of two more data sets showing the cross-sectional relationship between est. social media use and scores on different categories of life satisfaction. Understanding Society Dataset (just over 10,000 participants) including 10-15 y.o. individuals, and Millenium Cohort Study Dataset (over 11,000 participants) including 13-14 y.o. individuals. *Research Question/Part 2*

* Study then tested specific changes within individuals over time to see if there were developmental windows where sensitivity to social media’s impact on well-being was greater–method is called “longitudinal modeling” since subjects are followed and studied/surveyed repeatedly over a long period. Also included control variables of “time-invariant mean log household income” and “Index for Multiple Deprivation with freely estimated effects at different ages,” attempting to establish a more direct relationship between est. SMS use and life satisfaction ratings by excluding at least some aspects of socioeconomic impact.  
    * Results showed “**specific developmental windows where the data suggests estimated social media use and ratings of life satisfaction do predict each other**,” as predicted by the authors. Also found differences in age when these windows occur between males & females:  
    ![][image2]  
    * Using Akaike weights procedure to compare statistical likelihood of different models, the **life satisfaction \-\> social media model was found to likely be best if assumed constant between age and sex**, whereas the **social media \-\> life satisfaction relationship being allowed to vary based on age/sex was found to be most accurate** (again, indicating developmental windows for that correlation)  
    * Looking specifically at the social media \-\> life satisfaction results and highlighting statistically significant areas in grey:  
    ![][image3]  
        * **For females**, the authors observed a **period of sensitivity from ages 11-13**, “when increases in estimated social media use from expected levels predicted a decrease in life satisfaction ratings from expected levels one year later”   
            * Authors speculate that this **may be due to** maturation/**developmental processes** in puberty **that occur earlier for females** than males  
                * Highlights impact developmental changes in adolescence, and their specific timing, may have on social media’s link to well-being/life satisfaction  
        * **For males,** statistically significant, potential **period of sensitivity** is **from ages 14-15**, with similar social media use prediction of lowered satisfaction ratings  
        * Furthermore, the data showed **later increase in sensitivity for both sexes around age 19**  
            * Authors speculated this “**might be related to changes in the social environment such as a move away from home** and subsequent disruptions in social networks”  
        * In general, **paper suggests “further targeted investigation using data containing pubertal and social measurements”** to test whether authors’ speculation to explain window ages is accurate. See comment above
